name: Esther Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Esther, thank you for doing this. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and everything you say is confidential. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a water truck at the Kerrow bauxite mine, the red-dirt one out past the grain silos. I spray the haul roads all shift so the dust doesn't blind the truck drivers or get into everyone's lungs, and I fill up at the standpipe every forty minutes or so. It sounds simple, but you have to get the amount right: too little and there's dust, too much and a truck slides off the road. I'm still learning that, and the shift supervisor has had words with me twice. I like being out in the open, and I pray in the cab when the road's quiet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to the mine?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Daniel and I have a small cattle place, about four hundred acres, and two dry years and the beef price put us badly behind with the bank. I'd been keeping house and doing the parish office, but we needed real wages, so I applied here at fifty-six. We've less than a month's bills put by, and most of my pay goes to the farm loan. I use the AI on my phone every single day, by the way: for studying my truck ticket, the parish newsletter, the farm books, everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's that then, and get on with the day. At church I'd say the Lord gave us brains for a reason and it's still our job to use them. I'd probably write something light about it in the parish newsletter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a little sorry, because I like what it does for me. The AI helped me pass my truck ticket at fifty-six. I'd hate for people to decide it was all hype because it didn't take over the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving, keep studying for the next ticket so I can move onto haul trucks, which pays more. I'd keep using AI for the farm books to get on top of the loan. Nothing else changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit relieved for the others at work who were scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the AI helped you pass your truck ticket. How did that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd photograph the pages of the handbook and ask it to quiz me on the bus to the mine. When I got something wrong it explained it until I understood. I passed first try, and two of the young men didn't, which I won't pretend I didn't enjoy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would moving onto haul trucks mean for the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a hundred and twenty more a week, all of it onto the bank loan. That's maybe two years off the debt. Daniel would sleep better, and so would I.

S0.say: She'd say 'that's that' and get on with the day, telling church friends it's still our job to use our God-given brains, and perhaps write a light piece in the parish newsletter.
S0.think: She'd be a little sorry, because AI helped her pass her truck ticket at fifty-six and she doesn't want it dismissed as hype.
S0.do: Keeps driving and studies for a haul truck ticket worth about a hundred and twenty more a week. Uses AI for the farm books to get on top of the bank loan.
S0.feel: Calm, and relieved for frightened colleagues.
S0.quote: The AI helped me pass my truck ticket at fifty-six. I'd hate for people to decide it was all hype because it didn't take over the world.
S0.fieldNote: Esther is a traditional, church-going farm wife who is also the most enthusiastic AI user on her crew. She credits it with passing her ticket at fifty-six and enjoyed beating the young men. Her money goal is concrete: every extra dollar goes onto the farm loan.

steps.text: Keep driving the Kerrow water truck and study for the haul truck ticket
Use the phone AI on the farm books to get on top of the loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company has every right to run its business the best way it can, and it's up to us to make ourselves useful. I'd tell the women at work to start learning now. I'd not complain, complaining never paid a bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A water truck is the easiest thing in the world to automate, it just follows the roads and sprays. If I'm honest, my job is a sprinkler on wheels, and I'd be surprised if they need me in five years. So I'd want to be on the other side of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask straight away about the control room where they run the self-driving trucks, and do whatever course gets me there, using AI to study. I'd also start selling eggs and preserves online from the farm, which I've been meaning to do. And I'd keep every spare dollar going to the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly because of the loan, not the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'the other side of it'. Do you really think they'd put a fifty-eight-year-old in the control room?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Why not? I'm the one already using these programs every day. The young men can drive faster, but I can read a screen and I don't panic. If they don't pick me, I'll ask what I'd need to do to be picked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ray, on the grader. He's sixty and he won't touch a phone, he says it's the devil's toy. I've offered to help him and he says no thank you. I'd keep offering, and I'd pray for him.

S1.say: She'd say the company has every right to run its business as it sees fit and that workers must make themselves useful, urging the women at work to start learning now.
S1.think: She thinks her water truck is the easiest job to automate, a sprinkler on wheels, and wants to be on the control-room side of the change.
S1.do: Asks straight away about the self-driving truck control room and takes any course to get there, studying with AI. Starts selling eggs and preserves online and keeps putting every spare dollar on the farm loan.
S1.feel: Uneasy, mostly because of the farm loan rather than the robots.
S1.quote: If I'm honest, my job is a sprinkler on wheels, and I'd be surprised if they need me in five years.
S1.fieldNote: Esther combines free-market views ('the company has every right') with a cheerful plan to move first. She is blunt about her own job, calling it a sprinkler on wheels. Her unease comes from the farm debt, not fear of technology, and she keeps trying to help a colleague who refuses phones.

steps.text: Ask about control room training for the self-driving trucks straight away
Study for the control room course with the AI on the bus
Start selling eggs and preserves online from the farm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the clever computers come first and the hands later. Then the control room is the first thing gone. Well, there's my plan in the bin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At church I'd say the Lord gives us three years' warning, which is more than Noah got. I'd tell the women at work that the screen jobs go first this time, so learn something with your hands and use the AI to learn it. I'd still say the company has the right to run its business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my control room plan is finished before it starts, because watching screens is exactly the thinking work that goes in 2028. My water truck is hands-on, so I'd have till about 2031, but it's a sprinkler on wheels, so it'll be among the first robots. I'd be 63 with a farm loan, and the bank won't care whose fault it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the haul truck ticket in the first six months, because that's a hundred and twenty more a week straight onto the loan for three years. I'd let the AI run the farm books and the online shop properly, eggs, preserves and beef boxes, so the farm earns more on its own. And I'd sit down with our son and his wife to talk about them taking a share of the farm and the loan, before the bank comes asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but praying and working at the same time. I sleep fine, and then I wake up at three thinking about the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the haul truck ticket, if robots come for trucks in 2031 too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's three years of better pay, and three years of better pay is about a third of the loan. I'm not trying to keep the truck job forever. I'm trying to get the farm clear before the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Daniel think about your son taking a share?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd hate it at first, it's his father's land. But he'd rather share it with our boy than lose it to the bank. My husband Daniel would sooner sell me than sell those four hundred acres, and he'd say so himself.

S2.say: The Lord gives us three years' warning, which is more than Noah got. The screen jobs go first this time, so learn something with your hands and use the AI to learn it.
S2.think: My control room plan is finished before it starts, because watching screens is the thinking work that goes in 2028. The water truck lasts till about 2031, but it's a sprinkler on wheels, and I'd be 63 with a farm loan.
S2.do: Gets the haul truck ticket within six months and puts the extra 120 a week onto the farm loan for three years. Lets the AI run the farm books and an online shop for eggs, preserves and beef boxes, and talks to her son about taking a share of the farm and loan.
S2.feel: Anxious but praying and working at once. She sleeps, then wakes at three thinking about the bank.
S2.quote: I'm not trying to keep the truck job forever. I'm trying to get the farm clear before the robots come.
S2.fieldNote: Esther saw immediately that the control room she'd aimed for is screen work that goes first, and dropped it without fuss. Her new plan uses the three years of hands-on work purely to cut the farm loan. Family, not government, is her fallback, and she'd bring her son into the farm before the bank forces the issue.

steps.text: Get the haul truck ticket and put the extra 120 a week on the loan
Run an online shop for the farm's eggs, preserves and beef boxes
Ask her son and his wife to take a share of the farm and loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031 and 2034. I'd be sixty-six when the robots came. That's a different story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to prepare if you start now and don't feel sorry for yourself. I'd tell the women at work to use the AI to learn. I'd write about it in the parish newsletter, something cheerful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine, God willing. Five years of better pay pays down most of the farm, and by 2034 I'd be past retiring age. Five years is long enough for me to pay down the farm and be the grandmother who knows how the robots work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the haul truck ticket in the first year and put the extra on the loan. I'd build the online farm shop slowly, with the AI writing the descriptions. Once the loan's under control, I'd save about fifty a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more hopeful than not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still try for the control room?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe for a year or two, if they offered it. But with the thinking machines coming in 2031, I'd rather be on a truck. At least nobody expects a robot to drive a truck until 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Ray, the grader driver you worried about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ray would be retired by 2034, thank goodness. I'd stop nagging him about his phone. He's earned his peace.

S3.say: There's time to prepare if you start now and don't feel sorry for yourself. Use the AI to learn.
S3.think: I'd be fine, God willing, because five years of better pay pays down most of the farm and I'd be past retiring age by 2034. I'd be the grandmother who knows how the robots work.
S3.do: Gets the haul truck ticket in year one and puts the extra pay on the loan. Builds the online farm shop slowly with the AI writing descriptions, and saves about fifty a week once the loan is under control.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but more hopeful than not.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough for me to pay down the farm and be the grandmother who knows how the robots work.
S3.fieldNote: With robots due in 2034, Esther's working years and the farm loan both fit inside the window. She'd take the haul truck route over the control room, having noticed the screen jobs go first. Her worry for an older colleague eases because he'd be retired.

steps.text: Get the haul truck ticket in year one and put the extra on the loan
Build the online farm shop slowly, with the AI writing descriptions

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2036 and 2039. I'll be on the porch by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a blessing, and people should use it. I'd tell the young ones at church to get apprenticeships and learn the new tools as they go. I'd write a cheerful piece in the newsletter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd love it. I'd clear the farm loan over the decade, retire at sixty-six, and watch the robots arrive from the porch. With ten years I'd get the farm clear, retire on my own terms and still have time to boss the robots around a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the haul truck ticket, then maybe a control room course at a normal pace if it's offered. I'd clear the loan over the years and start saving for retirement. And I'd keep the online farm shop going as something for Daniel and me after we stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and quite pleased.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the farm itself change, with robots coming in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By then our son might want a robot for the fencing or the feeding. That's his business. I'd want the land clear of debt before he inherits it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd still worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The town, a little. When the mine runs itself, who buys at the grain store? But that's for younger people to sort out.

S4.say: Ten years is a blessing, and people should use it. The young ones should get apprenticeships and learn the new tools as they go.
S4.think: I'd love it: clear the farm loan over the decade, retire at sixty-six and watch the robots arrive from the porch. I'd still have time to boss the robots around a bit.
S4.do: Takes the haul truck ticket and perhaps a control room course at a normal pace, clears the farm loan over the years and starts saving for retirement. Keeps the online farm shop going as something for her and Daniel after they stop.
S4.quote: With ten years I'd get the farm clear, retire on my own terms and still have time to boss the robots around a bit.
S4.fieldNote: With a long timeline Esther is relaxed and focused on handing the farm to her son debt-free. She'd learn new systems at her own pace, enjoying it. Her only worry is the town's future once the mine runs itself.

steps.text: Take the haul truck ticket, then a control room course if offered
Clear the farm loan over the decade, then save for retirement
Keep the online farm shop going for her and Daniel's retirement

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because the control room job I'd train for goes to the computers first, and the bank wouldn't wait while I learned something new. What would help is the banks giving farm families a breathing space on loans when the jobs change, and the mine training older workers like me for the control room, not just the young ones. And keep the apprenticeships for the youngsters.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask about faith. People think a church lady can't love a computer, but I pray on the bus and then ask the AI to quiz me on my ticket. I don't see why it has to be one or the other.

headlineQuote: People think a church lady can't love a computer, but I pray on the bus and then ask the AI to quiz me on my ticket.
portrait: Esther Young is 58 and drives a water truck at the Kerrow bauxite mine, a job she took at fifty-six when dry years and low beef prices put her family's cattle farm behind with the bank. She has less than a month saved, and most of her pay goes on the farm loan. She is traditional and devout, and also uses AI every day; it helped her pass her truck ticket. She's calm or uneasy in the milder pictures, planning to move into the control room and sell farm produce online. AGI by 2028 makes her anxious because the control room is screen work that goes first, so she'd use her three hands-on years on a haul truck to pay down the loan and bring her son into the farm. With five or ten years she's hopeful about clearing the farm and retiring on her own terms.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because the control room job she'd train for goes first and the bank wouldn't wait while she learned something new.
whatWouldHelp: Banks giving farm families breathing space on loans when jobs change, and the mine training older workers for the control room as well as young ones.
